note: Shipped remediation playbooks. Add your own to data/playbooks_local.json (never overwritten by an update); see docs/PLAYBOOKS.md for the format.

playbooks.match: auto giveback is not enabled
playbooks.cause: Automatic giveback is off.
playbooks.impact: After a takeover the node ({node}) stays down until someone gives it back, leaving the pair without redundancy.
steps: 1. Check: storage failover show -fields auto-giveback,possible
2. Enable: storage failover modify -node * -auto-giveback true
3. Confirm: storage failover show -fields auto-giveback
options: Option A: Enable on all nodes (recommended).

ticket.window: Any; no outage
ticket.rollback: storage failover modify -node * -auto-giveback false

playbooks.match: ntp servers are not redundant
playbooks.cause: Fewer than two external NTP servers are configured.
playbooks.impact: Cluster time can drift, which breaks Kerberos/AD authentication, certificates, log correlation and SnapMirror schedules.
steps: 1. Check: cluster time-service ntp server show ; cluster time-service ntp status show
2. Add at least a second, independent source: cluster time-service ntp server create -server <ntp-server-2>
3. Use three or more servers where possible so a faulty source can be outvoted; prefer internal stratum 2-3 servers.
4. Check: cluster time-service ntp status show ; date
options: Option A: Three NTP servers, two internal and one external (recommended).

playbooks.match: one or more ntp servers are not responding
playbooks.cause: An NTP server configured on the cluster does not answer.
playbooks.impact: Cluster time can drift, which breaks Kerberos/AD authentication, certificates, log correlation and SnapMirror schedules.
steps: 1. Check: cluster time-service ntp server show ; cluster time-service ntp status show

2. Test reachability from the cluster network (UDP 123): network ping -lif <mgmt-lif> -vserver {cluster} -destination <ntp-server>; remove a dead server: cluster time-service ntp server delete -server <dead-ntp>
3. Use three or more servers where possible so a faulty source can be outvoted; prefer internal stratum 2-3 servers.
4. Check: cluster time-service ntp status show ; date
options: Option A: Three NTP servers, two internal and one external (recommended).

playbooks.match: vserver has a single dns server configured
playbooks.cause: SVM {svm} has one DNS server.
playbooks.impact: If it is unavailable, name resolution, AD authentication and SMB/NFS access fail.
steps: 1. Check: vserver services name-service dns show -vserver {svm}
2. Add the second server (keep the existing one first): vserver services name-service dns modify -vserver {svm} -domains <domain> -name-servers <dns1>,<dns2>
3. Check: vserver services name-service dns check -vserver {svm}
options: Option A: Two or more DNS servers in different locations (recommended).

playbooks.match: certificate validation is set to false for fabricpool
playbooks.cause: The FabricPool object store accepts any certificate.
playbooks.impact: Tiered data could be sent to an impostor endpoint (man-in-the-middle).
steps: 1. Check: storage aggregate object-store config show -fields server,ssl-enabled,is-certificate-validation-enabled
2. Install the CA that signed the object store certificate: security certificate install -type server-ca -vserver {cluster}
3. Turn validation on: storage aggregate object-store config modify -object-store-name <object-store> -is-certificate-validation-enabled true
4. Check the tiering still works: storage aggregate object-store show-space ; storage aggregate show -fields tiering-policy
options: Option A: Install the CA and enable validation (recommended).

playbooks.match: cluster peering encryption not enabled
playbooks.cause: Replication traffic between the clusters is not encrypted.
playbooks.impact: SnapMirror data and metadata cross the network in clear text.
steps: 1. Check: cluster peer show -fields encryption-protocol-proposed,encryption-protocol,auth-status-admin

2. Enable on this cluster: cluster peer modify -cluster <peer-cluster> -auth-status-admin use-authentication -encryption-protocol-proposed tls-psk  (do the same on the peer; the passphrase is generated and exchanged for you in 9.6 and later).
3. Check: cluster peer show -fields encryption-protocol ; snapmirror show -fields status
options: Option A: TLS-PSK on every peer relationship (recommended).
playbooks.thirdParty: Do the change on both clusters in the same window; a mismatch stops transfers until both agree.

ticket.window: Both clusters in the same window; transfers pause until both agree
ticket.rollback: cluster peer modify -cluster <peer> -encryption-protocol-proposed none (both sides).

playbooks.match: system has not converted to either netapp license fi?le \(nlf\)
playbooks.cause: The cluster still has 28-character license keys instead of NetApp license files.
playbooks.impact: Old keys are no longer issued; capacity and feature changes need NLF, and entitlement checks can fail after an upgrade.
steps: 1. List what is installed: system license show -fields package,type,expiration
2. Sign in to the NetApp Support Site (My Support, Software Licenses), enter the cluster serial numbers (system node show -fields serialnumber for {cluster}) and download the NLF for each.
3. Install: system license add -license-code <contents of the NLF>  (one per serial number).
4. Check: system license show-status
options: Option A: Install NLF for every node serial (recommended).

playbooks.match: multi-admin verification not enabled
playbooks.cause: Multi-admin verification (MAV) is off, so one administrator can run destructive commands alone.
playbooks.impact: Ransomware or an insider can delete snapshots, volumes or the configuration backup without a second person approving it.
steps: 1. Pick two or more administrators who will approve (never the requester alone) and confirm their e-mail addresses for notification.
2. On {cluster}, create the approval group: security multi-admin-verify approval-group create -name mav-approvers -approvers <admin1>,<admin2> -email <approvers@example.com>
3. Turn MAV on with the group and the number of approvals needed: security multi-admin-verify modify -approval-groups mav-approvers -required-approvers 1 -enabled true

4. Protect the destructive operations, for example: security multi-admin-verify rule create -operation "volume delete" ; security multi-admin-verify rule create -operation "volume snapshot delete" ; security multi-admin-verify rule create -operation "snapmirror delete"
5. Check: security multi-admin-verify show ; security multi-admin-verify rule show ; then test with a non-critical volume so the approval flow is known before it is needed.

belowMin.cause: Multi-admin verification needs ONTAP 9.11.1 or later; {cluster} runs {version}.
belowMin.impact: A single compromised or mistaken administrator can delete volumes, snapshots or the cluster configuration with no second approval.
steps: 1. Plan the upgrade of {cluster} to a release that supports multi-admin verification (9.11.1 or later, 9.12.1 or later recommended).
2. Enable it once the cluster is upgraded (steps below).

options: Option A: Enable now with at least two approvers (recommended).
Option B: Start with fewer protected operations (volume delete, snapshot delete) and add the rest after the first month.
playbooks.thirdParty: Automation that deletes volumes or snapshots (backup software, scripts) will wait for approval once a rule covers the operation; list those accounts first.

ticket.window: Any; no outage
ticket.rollback: Disable with: security multi-admin-verify modify -enabled false (this itself needs approval once rules exist). Remove a rule with security multi-admin-verify rule delete.

playbooks.match: cluster config(?:uration)? backups are not being pushed remotely
playbooks.cause: The cluster configuration backups are written only to the cluster itself.
playbooks.impact: If {cluster} is lost or its root volume corrupted, there is no off-cluster copy to rebuild the configuration from.
steps: 1. Choose an HTTP(S), FTP or SCP-capable server that is not on {cluster} (a hardened backup host).
2. Set the destination: system configuration backup settings modify -destination https://<backup-server>/<path> -username <user>  (it prompts for the password).
3. Check the setting and the schedule: system configuration backup settings show ; system configuration backup show
4. Take one now and confirm it arrives: system configuration backup create -node {node} -backup-type cluster ; then list it on the backup server.
5. Keep at least one copy off-site and test a restore procedure once (docs.netapp.com, "Back up and restore cluster configurations").
options: Option A: HTTPS or SCP destination (recommended).
Option B: FTP only if the network is isolated; credentials are sent in clear.

playbooks.match: cluster log forwarding not configured
playbooks.cause: Audit and event logs stay on the cluster only.
playbooks.impact: Logs cannot be correlated centrally and are lost with the cluster or on rollover; an attacker with admin access could remove local evidence.
steps: 1. Choose the syslog/SIEM collector and protocol (tcp-encrypted is recommended; it needs the server certificate chain installed with: security certificate install -type server-ca -vserver {cluster}).
2. On {cluster}: cluster log-forwarding create -destination <siem-host> -port 6514 -protocol tcp-encrypted -facility user -verify-server true
3. Check: cluster log-forwarding show
4. Make sure audit events you need are generated (for example: security audit show ; vserver audit show -vserver {svm}).
options: Option A: tcp-encrypted with server verification (recommended).
Option B: udp-unencrypted only on an isolated management network.

playbooks.match: tamperproof snapshot not enabled
playbooks.cause: Snapshots are not locked, so they can be deleted before they expire.
playbooks.impact: A compromised administrator account can remove every recovery point.
steps: 1. Initialise the SnapLock Compliance clock once per node (it cannot be reset afterwards): snaplock compliance-clock initialize -node {node}  (repeat for each node; check: snaplock compliance-clock show)
2. For each critical volume, enable snapshot locking: volume modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -snapshot-locking-enabled true
3. Create snapshots with a retention lock: volume snapshot create -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -snapshot <name> -snaplock-expiry-time "<yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss>"  (or set a policy that applies it).
4. Check: volume show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -fields snapshot-locking-enabled ; volume snapshot show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -fields snaplock-expiry-time
5. Keep capacity headroom: locked snapshots cannot be deleted to free space.

belowMin.cause: Tamperproof snapshots need ONTAP 9.12.1 or later; {cluster} runs {version}.
belowMin.impact: Snapshots can be deleted by an administrator (or malware with admin access) before their retention ends.
steps: 1. Plan the upgrade of {cluster} to 9.12.1 or later.
2. Then lock the snapshots of critical volumes (steps below).

options: Option A: Lock the snapshots of the most critical volumes first (recommended).
Option B: Replicate to a SnapLock vault instead (SnapVault to a Compliance volume).
playbooks.thirdParty: Backup software that prunes snapshots will fail on locked ones; align its retention with the lock.

ticket.window: Any; the compliance clock cannot be reset
ticket.rollback: Locked snapshots cannot be removed before their expiry; the compliance clock is permanent. Confirm retention with the data owner before applying.

playbooks.match: native fpolicy is not enabled
playbooks.cause: Native FPolicy is not enabled on the SVMs that serve NAS protocols.
playbooks.impact: Known ransomware file extensions and unwanted file types are not blocked at the storage layer.
steps: 1. Create the event for the SMB operations to watch (on SVM {svm}): vserver fpolicy policy event create -vserver {svm} -event-name block-events -protocol cifs -file-operations create,rename,write -filters first-write
2. Create the native policy: vserver fpolicy policy create -vserver {svm} -policy-name native-block -events block-events -engine native -is-mandatory false
3. Define what to block: vserver fpolicy policy scope create -vserver {svm} -policy-name native-block -volumes-to-include "*" -file-extensions-to-include "<comma-separated extensions>"
4. Enable it: vserver fpolicy enable -vserver {svm} -policy-name native-block -sequence-number 1
5. Check: vserver fpolicy show -vserver {svm} ; vserver fpolicy policy show -vserver {svm}
6. Repeat for every SVM that serves NAS.
options: Option A: Native FPolicy for blocking by extension (recommended starting point).
Option B: External FPolicy engine with a partner product for deeper inspection.
playbooks.thirdParty: Tell backup and migration teams: a blocked extension fails the write for them as well.

playbooks.match: fips 140-2 (?:compliance )?is disabled
playbooks.cause: FIPS 140-2 mode for SSL/TLS is not enabled on the cluster.
playbooks.impact: Management and data services may negotiate algorithms that are not FIPS-approved; regulated customers may fail an audit.
steps: 1. Check clients first: FIPS mode disables TLS 1.0/1.1 and non-approved ciphers, so list the management tools and integrations that connect to {cluster}.
2. See the current setting: security config show -interface SSL
3. Enable in a change window: security config modify -interface SSL -is-fips-enabled true  (review the confirmation; some services restart their TLS listeners).
4. Test the management interfaces, Active IQ Unified Manager, SnapCenter, backup and monitoring connections.
options: Option A: Enable now if no client needs older TLS (recommended for regulated data).
Option B: Upgrade or reconfigure the old clients first, then enable.

ticket.window: Maintenance window; TLS listeners restart
ticket.rollback: security config modify -interface SSL -is-fips-enabled false

playbooks.match: data-at-rest encryption is not enabled
playbooks.cause: Data at rest is not encrypted by NetApp Volume Encryption or self-encrypting drives.
playbooks.impact: Removed drives or shelves, and returned or decommissioned media, can be read.
steps: 1. Choose the key manager: onboard (security key-manager onboard enable) or an external KMIP server (security key-manager external enable -vserver {cluster} -key-servers <kmip-host>:5696 -client-cert <cert> -server-ca-certs <ca>).
2. With the onboard manager, store the passphrase and immediately back it up: security key-manager onboard show-backup  (keep it off the cluster).

3. Encrypt new volumes: volume create ... -encrypt true. Convert existing volumes in place: volume encryption conversion start -vserver {svm} -volume <volume>, check with volume encryption conversion show.
4. Check: volume show -fields encrypt ; security key-manager key query
options: Option A: NVE on all volumes with an external key manager (recommended).
Option B: NVE with the onboard key manager where no KMIP server exists.
playbooks.thirdParty: Deduplication savings across volumes are unchanged for NVE from 9.6, but plan a brief performance check on very latency-sensitive volumes.

ticket.window: Off-peak; conversion runs in the background
ticket.rollback: Encryption conversion cannot be undone in place; move the volume to an unencrypted aggregate with volume move start -encrypt-destination false if required.

playbooks.match: export rule is using a client match of 0\.0\.0\.0\/0
playbooks.cause: Export policy {policy} on SVM {svm} allows every client address.
playbooks.impact: Any host on a reachable network can mount the data; this is one of the most common causes of unintended NFS exposure.
steps: 1. List the rules: vserver export-policy rule show -vserver {svm} -policyname {policy} -fields ruleindex,clientmatch,rorule,rwrule,superuser
2. Identify the real clients (the application owners, or NFS client addresses from: network connections active show -vserver {svm} ; statistics may help).
3. Narrow the rule: vserver export-policy rule modify -vserver {svm} -policyname {policy} -ruleindex <n> -clientmatch <client-subnet-or-hostgroup> -rorule sys -rwrule sys -superuser none

4. Add rules for each client group instead of one open rule: vserver export-policy rule create -vserver {svm} -policyname {policy} -clientmatch <subnet> -rorule sys -rwrule sys -superuser none -protocol nfs

5. Test a mount from an allowed and a blocked host, and check: vserver export-policy check-access -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -client-ip <ip> -authentication-method sys -protocol nfs3 -access-type read
6. Repeat for the other policies the finding names on this SVM.
options: Option A: Replace 0.0.0.0/0 with the client subnets (recommended).
Option B: Keep the rule read-only with root squash if clients cannot be listed yet, and record an exception.

ticket.window: Business hours with the application owner present; a wrong client list blocks access
ticket.rollback: Restore the clientmatch recorded in step 1: vserver export-policy rule modify -vserver <svm> -policyname <policy> -ruleindex <n> -clientmatch 0.0.0.0/0

playbooks.match: enable ontap anti-ransomware
playbooks.cause: Autonomous Ransomware Protection (ARP) is not enabled on the volumes.
playbooks.impact: A ransomware encryption wave is not detected or answered with an automatic snapshot.
steps: 1. ARP needs a license (included in ONTAP One): system license show -package *

2. Start in learning mode on a volume: security anti-ransomware volume dry-run -vserver {svm} -volume <volume>  (9.10.1 to 9.12.1: volume modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -anti-ransomware-state dry-run)
3. After 30 days of normal workload (or as ONTAP advises), switch to active: security anti-ransomware volume enable -vserver {svm} -volume <volume>
4. Check: security anti-ransomware volume show -vserver {svm} ; and add an alert path: event notification destination show

belowMin.cause: Autonomous Ransomware Protection needs ONTAP 9.10.1 or later; {cluster} runs {version}.
belowMin.impact: Encryption-based attacks are not detected at the storage layer.
steps: 1. Plan the upgrade of {cluster} to 9.10.1 or later (9.13.1 or later turns learning on automatically for new volumes).

options: Option A: Learn for 30 days, then enable active mode (recommended).
Option B: Enable active mode at once on volumes with stable, well-known workloads.

playbooks.match: smb signing and encryption not enabled|smb signing is disabled
playbooks.cause: SMB signing and encryption are not required on SVM {svm}.
playbooks.impact: SMB traffic can be tampered with or read in transit (relay and man-in-the-middle attacks).
steps: 1. Check clients: Windows 7/2008 R2 and older, and some appliances, cannot sign with SMB 3 encryption. Inventory with: vserver cifs session show -vserver {svm} -fields protocol-version,windows-user,address
2. Require signing: vserver cifs security modify -vserver {svm} -is-signing-required true

3. Allow AES encryption (SMB 3): vserver cifs security modify -vserver {svm} -is-aes-encryption-enabled true ; to force encryption on a share: vserver cifs share modify -vserver {svm} -share-name <share> -share-properties encrypt-data
4. Check: vserver cifs security show -vserver {svm} -fields is-signing-required,is-aes-encryption-enabled
options: Option A: Require signing everywhere; require encryption on sensitive shares (recommended).
Option B: Require signing only, if old clients cannot use SMB 3 encryption.

ticket.window: Maintenance window; old clients may fail to connect
ticket.rollback: vserver cifs security modify -vserver <svm> -is-signing-required false

playbooks.match: vserver has multiple default gateways with the same metric
playbooks.cause: SVM {svm} has two or more default routes with the same metric.
playbooks.impact: ONTAP cannot choose a gateway, so DNS and other name-service lookups can fail intermittently.
steps: 1. List the routes: network route show -vserver {svm} -destination 0.0.0.0/0

2. Decide which gateway is primary. Give the secondary a higher metric: network route delete -vserver {svm} -destination 0.0.0.0/0 -gateway <secondary-gw> ; network route create -vserver {svm} -destination 0.0.0.0/0 -gateway <secondary-gw> -metric 30

3. Keep the primary at the lower metric (for example 20). ONTAP has no command to change a route's metric: delete the route and create it again: network route delete -vserver {svm} -destination 0.0.0.0/0 -gateway <primary-gw> ; network route create -vserver {svm} -destination 0.0.0.0/0 -gateway <primary-gw> -metric 20
4. Check: network route show -vserver {svm} ; and a name lookup: vserver services name-service dns check -vserver {svm}
options: Option A: One default gateway, or two with different metrics (recommended).

ticket.window: Maintenance window; routing changes briefly
ticket.rollback: Recreate the removed route with its recorded gateway and metric: network route create -vserver <svm> -destination 0.0.0.0/0 -gateway <gw> -metric <m>

playbooks.match: vscan is not enabled
playbooks.cause: Virus scanning (Vscan) is not enabled on SVM {svm}.
playbooks.impact: Files written over SMB are not scanned on access.
steps: 1. Have the antivirus (AV) servers with the NetApp-supported connector ready, and an SMB account they use.
2. Create a scanner pool: vserver vscan scanner-pool create -vserver {svm} -scanner-pool vscan-pool -hostnames <av-server1>,<av-server2> -privileged-users <domain\avuser> -scanner-policy primary

3. Apply a policy and enable: vserver vscan scanner-pool apply-policy -vserver {svm} -scanner-pool vscan-pool -scanner-policy primary ; vserver vscan on-access-policy create -vserver {svm} -policy-name default-cifs -protocol CIFS -scan-files-with-no-ext true ; vserver vscan enable -vserver {svm}
4. Check: vserver vscan connection-status show -vserver {svm} ; vserver vscan show -vserver {svm}
options: Option A: On-access scanning with two AV servers (recommended).
Option B: On-demand scanning only, scheduled off-hours.
playbooks.thirdParty: Size the AV servers: scan latency adds to file open time.

playbooks.match: intercluster peer remote ip address configuration
playbooks.cause: A cluster peer lists too few remote intercluster addresses.
playbooks.impact: If that one address or node is down, replication to this cluster stops.
steps: 1. Check: cluster peer show -instance ; cluster peer show -fields peer-addresses,availability
2. On the remote cluster list every node's intercluster LIF: network interface show -role intercluster -fields address,home-node
3. Add one address per remote node: cluster peer modify -cluster <peer-cluster> -peer-addrs <ip-node1>,<ip-node2>,<ip-node3>,<ip-node4>
4. Check: cluster peer show -fields peer-addresses,availability ; cluster peer health show
options: Option A: List one intercluster LIF per remote node (recommended).

playbooks.match: enable compaction to support more workloads
playbooks.cause: Data compaction is not enabled on volumes that would benefit.
playbooks.impact: Less effective capacity than the system can provide; earlier than necessary capacity purchase.
steps: 1. Check: volume efficiency show -vserver {svm} -fields state,compression,inline-compression,data-compaction
2. Enable (all-flash and Flash Pool aggregates): volume efficiency modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -data-compaction true
3. Apply to existing data in the background: volume efficiency start -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -scan-old-data true
4. Check savings after the scan: volume efficiency show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -fields progress ; volume show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -fields sis-space-saved
options: Option A: Enable on all general-purpose volumes (recommended).
Option B: Skip volumes that already hold compressed or encrypted data.

playbooks.match: enable compression to support more workloads
playbooks.cause: Compression is not enabled on volumes that would benefit.
playbooks.impact: Less effective capacity than the system can provide; earlier than necessary capacity purchase.
steps: 1. Check: volume efficiency show -vserver {svm} -fields state,compression,inline-compression,data-compaction
2. Enable inline and background compression: volume efficiency modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -compression true -inline-compression true
3. Apply to existing data in the background: volume efficiency start -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -scan-old-data true
4. Check savings after the scan: volume efficiency show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -fields progress ; volume show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -fields sis-space-saved
options: Option A: Enable on all general-purpose volumes (recommended).
Option B: Skip volumes that already hold compressed or encrypted data.

playbooks.match: nse\) drives or self encrypting drives \(sed\) are present but not|netapp storage encryption \(nse\) drives
playbooks.cause: Self-encrypting drives are installed but their encryption is not activated.
playbooks.impact: The drives encrypt nothing until a key manager supplies authentication keys; removed drives remain readable.
steps: 1. Check: storage encryption disk show -fields data-key-id,fips-key-id
2. Set up a key manager if none exists: security key-manager external enable (KMIP) or security key-manager onboard enable.
3. Take ownership of the drives with an authentication key: storage encryption disk modify -disk * -data-key-id <key-id>  (the key manager creates the ID).
4. Check: storage encryption disk show -fields data-key-id ; security key-manager key query
options: Option A: External key manager (recommended).
Option B: Onboard key manager when no KMIP server exists.

ticket.window: Off-peak; conversion runs in the background
ticket.rollback: Encryption conversion cannot be undone in place; move the volume to an unencrypted aggregate with volume move start -encrypt-destination false if required.

playbooks.match: consolidate storage to reduce the number of nodes or shelves|low capacity utilization for production system
playbooks.cause: The system runs well below its capacity and performance limits.
playbooks.impact: Power, cooling, support and licensing are paid for equipment that is mostly idle.
steps: 1. Measure real use over time: storage aggregate show -fields size,usedsize,percent-used ; statistics show-periodic -object node -instance {node} -interval 5 -iterations 12
2. Decide what can move: volume move start -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -destination-aggregate <aggr> (non-disruptive) to free nodes or shelves, or retire the system in a refresh.
3. Review contracts before changing hardware: the support end date and the cost per shelf are in the Contracts section.
options: Option A: Consolidate at the next refresh.
Option B: Keep as is where the headroom is deliberate growth capacity.

playbooks.match: platform .+ reached end-of-availability
playbooks.cause: {model|This platform} is no longer sold{?eoa} (end of availability {eoa}){/?}{?eos} and NetApp support ends {eos}{/?}.
playbooks.impact: Spare parts, support and new ONTAP releases stop at end of support; a hardware failure after that date may not be repairable under contract.
steps: 1. Record what is installed on {cluster}: system node show -fields model,serialnumber,uptime ; storage shelf show -fields model ; and the support end dates in the Contracts section of this report.

2. Choose the replacement in the same family with NetApp's Hardware Universe (hwu.netapp.com), sized from current use: storage aggregate show -fields size,usedsize ; statistics show-periodic -object node -interval 5 -iterations 12.
3. Check the target ONTAP release supports both the old and the new controllers (needed for a non-disruptive swap) in the NetApp Interoperability Matrix.

4. Keep the existing shelves where the new controllers support them, and move the data without downtime: controller upgrade by aggregate relocation (ARL) with storage aggregate relocation start -node {node} -destination <new-node> -aggregate-list <aggr>, or volume move start -vserver <svm> -volume <vol> -destination-aggregate <new-aggr> to a new cluster in the same cluster peer.

5. {?eos}Plan to finish before {eos}; if that is not possible, extend support while the migration is under way and keep the quote date in the change record.{:}Extend support while the migration is under way.{/?}
options: Option A: Replace the controllers, keep shelves where supported (ARL).
Option B: Move the workload to a new cluster with SnapMirror and retire this one.
Option C: Extend support for a bounded period when the refresh is already budgeted.

ticket.window: Planned project; CAB approval and a migration window
ticket.rollback: Keep the source controllers and data intact until the new ones are verified; aggregate relocation can be reversed with storage aggregate relocation start in the other direction.

playbooks.match: enable real-time power consumption reporting through netapp cloud insights|data infrastructure insights
playbooks.cause: Cluster power use is estimated, not measured.
playbooks.impact: Sustainability reporting shows modelled figures, so energy savings cannot be proven.
steps: 1. Create a read-only account for the collector on {cluster}: security login create -vserver {cluster} -user-or-group-name insights-ro -application http -authentication-method password -role readonly ; security login create -vserver {cluster} -user-or-group-name insights-ro -application ontapi -authentication-method password -role readonly

2. In NetApp Data Infrastructure Insights (Cloud Insights) add an acquisition unit on a host that can reach the cluster management LIF, then add the ONTAP data collector for {cluster} with that account.
3. Allow the collector through the firewall: HTTPS (443) to the cluster management LIF.
4. Check after the first poll: the cluster shows measured power in Data Infrastructure Insights and the finding clears in Active IQ.
options: Option A: Data Infrastructure Insights collector (recommended).
Option B: Active IQ Digital Advisor sustainability estimates only.

playbooks.match: discover the cluster in bluexp
playbooks.cause: The cluster is not added to NetApp BlueXP.
playbooks.impact: Sustainability and carbon figures are not available for it.
steps: 1. In BlueXP choose Storage > Canvas > Add working environment > On-premises ONTAP > Discover, and enter {cluster}'s management address.

2. Use an account with the admin role for discovery, or a read-only account for monitoring only: security login create -vserver {cluster} -user-or-group-name bluexp-ro -application http -authentication-method password -role readonly
3. Install a BlueXP Connector in the network that can reach the cluster management LIF (HTTPS 443).
options: Option A: Discover with a read-only account (recommended).

playbooks.match: enable cluster switch log collection|switch is not setup for periodic data collection
playbooks.cause: Log collection from the cluster switches is off.
playbooks.impact: Switch problems (CRC errors, link flaps, firmware faults) are not reported to NetApp and are harder to diagnose.
steps: 1. List the switches ONTAP monitors: system switch ethernet show

2. Give ONTAP access to the switch logs: system switch ethernet log setup-password  (it asks for the switch's full name as listed by system switch ethernet show, and for the switch admin password; repeat for each switch).
3. Turn on the hourly collection of periodic data for each switch: system switch ethernet log modify -device <switch> -periodic-enabled true
4. Check: system switch ethernet log show ; system switch ethernet show
options: Option A: Enable on all cluster and storage switches (recommended).

playbooks.match: enable cifs aes kerberos encryption
playbooks.cause: The CIFS servers still allow RC4 for Kerberos.
playbooks.impact: Microsoft is retiring RC4 support in Active Directory; machine accounts without AES will fail to authenticate once it is enforced.
steps: 1. Check: vserver cifs security show -vserver {svm} -fields kerberos-clock-skew,is-aes-encryption-enabled,kerberos-ticket-age
2. Enable AES: vserver cifs security modify -vserver {svm} -is-aes-encryption-enabled true

3. In Active Directory, make sure the SVM's computer account supports AES: Get-ADComputer <cifs-server> -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes (24 or 28 includes AES128 and AES256) and fix with Set-ADComputer if needed.
4. Test an SMB mount from a Windows client and check the session: vserver cifs session show -vserver {svm} -fields auth-mechanism
options: Option A: Enable AES now (recommended).

ticket.window: Any; no outage
ticket.rollback: vserver cifs security modify -vserver <svm> -is-aes-encryption-enabled false

playbooks.match: detect expired certificates|certificate.*expired|expired certificate
playbooks.cause: One or more certificates on the cluster have expired or are about to.
playbooks.impact: TLS clients, management tools and replication peers reject an expired certificate; the failure is sudden.
steps: 1. Find them: security certificate show -vserver * -fields common-name,type,expiration,serial -expiration <"mm/dd/yyyy">  (use today's date plus 60 days), and security certificate show-truststore for the trusted CAs.
2. Create a request: security certificate generate-csr -common-name <fqdn> -size 3072 -hash-function SHA256 ; have your CA sign it.
3. Install: security certificate install -type server -vserver {scope} (paste the signed certificate and chain).
4. Use it: security ssl modify -vserver {scope} -common-name <fqdn> -server-enabled true -serial <new-serial> -ca <ca-name>
5. Remove the expired one once nothing references it: security certificate delete -vserver {scope} -common-name <fqdn> -ca <ca> -type server -serial <old-serial>
options: Option A: Replace with CA-signed certificates and set a calendar reminder 60 days before expiry (recommended).

ticket.window: Maintenance window; clients reconnect
ticket.rollback: Re-apply the previous certificate: security ssl modify -vserver <svm> -serial <old-serial> -server-enabled true (before deleting it).

playbooks.match: broadcast domain (?:contains ports from multiple vlans|has non-optimal layer two reachability)|ipspace configuration check
playbooks.cause: A broadcast domain on {cluster} contains ports that cannot reach each other at layer 2.
playbooks.impact: LIF failover to a port without the same network leaves the LIF unreachable.
steps: 1. See the layout: network port broadcast-domain show ; network port show -fields broadcast-domain,mtu,vlan-id
2. Check what ONTAP sees: network port reachability show -detail
3. Let ONTAP repair the membership, one port at a time: network port reachability repair -node {node} -port <port>  (review the planned change first).
4. For ports on different VLANs, use one broadcast domain per VLAN: network port broadcast-domain create -broadcast-domain <name> -mtu 1500 -ports {node}:<port>
5. Check failover works: network interface show -failover ; network interface revert -vserver * -lif *
options: Option A: Repair with ONTAP reachability, then verify failover (recommended).

ticket.window: Maintenance window; ports change membership
ticket.rollback: Move the port back: network port broadcast-domain add-ports / remove-ports with the layout recorded in step 1.

playbooks.match: enable deduplication to support more workloads
playbooks.cause: Deduplication is not enabled on volumes that would benefit.
playbooks.impact: Less effective capacity than the system can provide.
steps: 1. Check: volume efficiency show -vserver {svm} -fields state,policy,schedule
2. Enable: volume efficiency on -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> ; volume efficiency modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -policy auto
3. Run on existing data: volume efficiency start -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -scan-old-data true
4. Check: volume efficiency show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> ; volume show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -fields sis-space-saved
options: Option A: Enable on all general-purpose volumes (recommended).

playbooks.match: continuously-available cifs share property configured
playbooks.cause: The continuously-available property is set on a share that does not need it.
playbooks.impact: It is for Hyper-V and SQL Server over SMB; on ordinary shares it adds state and can slow failover.
steps: 1. List shares with it: vserver cifs share show -vserver {svm} -fields share-properties
2. For shares that do not host Hyper-V or SQL Server workloads: vserver cifs share properties remove -vserver {svm} -share-name <share> -share-properties continuously-available
3. Check: vserver cifs share show -vserver {svm} -share-name <share> -fields share-properties
options: Option A: Remove it except for Hyper-V and SQL over SMB shares (recommended).

playbooks.match: enable cold data monitoring|inactive data reporting
playbooks.cause: Inactive data reporting is off for aggregate {aggr}.
playbooks.impact: The system cannot show how much data is cold, so the saving from tiering (FabricPool) cannot be sized.
steps: 1. Check: storage aggregate show -aggregate {aggr} -fields is-inactive-data-reporting-enabled
2. Enable it (no outage, small background cost): storage aggregate modify -aggregate {aggr} -is-inactive-data-reporting-enabled true

3. Wait about 31 days for the first full picture, then read it per volume: volume show -vserver <svm> -volume <volume> -fields performance-tier-inactive-user-data,performance-tier-inactive-user-data-percent
4. Use the numbers to decide which volumes to tier (see the tiering procedure).
options: Option A: Enable on all SSD aggregates (recommended).

playbooks.match: enable tiering to reduce on-prem storage|not using the fabricpool feature
playbooks.cause: {cluster} does not tier cold data to object storage.
playbooks.impact: Premium flash holds data nobody reads, which costs space, power and a refresh earlier than necessary.
steps: 1. Size it first: enable inactive data reporting (storage aggregate modify -aggregate <aggr> -is-inactive-data-reporting-enabled true) and read the cold share per volume after 31 days.

2. Add the object store (StorageGRID, S3 or a cloud): storage aggregate object-store config create -object-store-name tier1 -provider-type <StorageGRID|AWS_S3|Azure_Cloud|GoogleCloud> -server <endpoint> -container-name <bucket> -access-key <key> -secret-password <secret> -is-ssl-enabled true -is-certificate-validation-enabled true
3. Attach it to the aggregate: storage aggregate object-store attach -aggregate <aggr> -object-store-name tier1  (an attach is permanent for the aggregate).
4. Tier chosen volumes: volume modify -vserver <svm> -volume <volume> -tiering-policy auto -tiering-minimum-cooling-days 31  (snapshot-only for backup data).
5. Check: storage aggregate object-store show-space ; volume show -fields tiering-policy,performance-tier-inactive-user-data
options: Option A: StorageGRID as the tier (recommended where available).
Option B: Public cloud object storage.
playbooks.thirdParty: Network: the cluster intercluster LIFs must reach the object store; plan bandwidth for the first tier-out.

playbooks.match: enable flexcache to reduce
playbooks.cause: FlexCache is not used for data that is read from many places.
playbooks.impact: Remote sites and busy clients read the same data over the WAN or from one overloaded volume.
steps: 1. Pick the volume that is read widely and rarely changed (software distribution, reference data, home directories read from several sites).

2. If the cache is on another cluster, peer first: cluster peer create -peer-addrs <ic-lif-ips> ; vserver peer create -vserver {svm} -peer-vserver <origin-svm> -peer-cluster <origin-cluster> -applications flexcache
3. Create the cache: volume flexcache create -vserver {svm} -volume <cache-volume> -aggr-list <aggr> -size <size> -origin-vserver <origin-svm> -origin-volume <origin-volume> -junction-path /<path>
4. Check: volume flexcache show ; volume flexcache origin show-caches -origin-vserver <origin-svm> -origin-volume <origin-volume>
5. Point the clients at the cache path and compare latency before and after.
options: Option A: A cache per remote site for read-mostly data (recommended).
Option B: Leave it; this is an optimisation, not a defect.
playbooks.thirdParty: FlexCache is an opportunity, not a fault; apply it where a measurable read problem exists.

playbooks.match: flexclone license installed but never used|instantly replicate data files, luns
playbooks.cause: The FlexClone license is installed and no clone has been made.
playbooks.impact: Test and development copies take full space and time when a clone would take almost none.
steps: 1. Confirm the license: system license show -package FlexClone
2. Make a writable copy of a volume from a snapshot: volume clone create -vserver {svm} -flexclone <clone-name> -parent-volume <volume> -parent-snapshot <snapshot> -junction-path /<clone-name>
3. Check: volume clone show ; volume show -vserver {svm} -volume <clone-name> -fields size,used
4. Split it from its parent only when it must outlive it: volume clone split start -vserver {svm} -flexclone <clone-name>
options: Option A: Use clones for test, development and recovery testing (recommended).
Option B: Ignore; informational.
playbooks.thirdParty: An optimisation: the finding is information that a licensed feature is unused.

playbooks.match: dqp package downrev
playbooks.cause: The Disk Qualification Package (DQP) on the cluster is older than NetApp's current one.
playbooks.impact: New drive models or firmware are not recognised correctly, and drive handling can be wrong.
steps: 1. Download the current DQP zip from the NetApp Support Site (Downloads > Firmware > Disk Qualification Package) and put it on a web server the cluster can reach.
2. Install it on every node: storage firmware download -node * -package-url http://<web-server>/<qual_devices_v3>.zip
3. Check the drives are still recognised: storage disk show -broken ; storage disk show -fields firmware-revision,model
options: Option A: Install the current package (recommended, non-disruptive).
playbooks.thirdParty: Do not install a DQP built for a different ONTAP family than the cluster runs.

playbooks.match: maximum limit reached for inflight operations
playbooks.cause: NFS clients are sending more operations at once than ONTAP allows per connection.
playbooks.impact: ONTAP throttles the requests, so applications see latency spikes.
steps: 1. Clients named by the finding: {clients|see the finding detail}.

2. On each Linux client, cap the RPC slot table at the NetApp-recommended value: echo "options sunrpc tcp_max_slot_table_entries=128" > /etc/modprobe.d/sunrpc.conf  (and the same for tcp_slot_table_entries), then unmount, reload the sunrpc module or reboot the client, and remount.
3. Check on the cluster that the over-limit event stops: event log show -message-name nblade.execsOverLimit
4. If many clients are affected, check the workload: statistics show -object nfsv3 -counter nfsv3_ops ; statistics top client show -sort-key total_ops
options: Option A: Limit slot entries on the named clients (recommended).
Option B: Spread the clients across more LIFs and nodes.

playbooks.match: inline efficiency features are not enabled on non-root volumes
playbooks.cause: Inline efficiency is off on volumes of {cluster} ({vols}).
playbooks.impact: Savings are lost on new writes and have to be recovered later by background jobs.
steps: 1. Check: volume efficiency show -vserver {vsvm} -volume {vvol} -fields inline-dedupe,inline-compression,data-compaction
2. Enable: volume efficiency modify -vserver {vsvm} -volume {vvol} -inline-dedupe true -inline-compression true -data-compaction true
3. Repeat for the other volumes the finding lists.
options: Option A: Enable all three (recommended on all-flash).

playbooks.match: two intercluster lifs on two ports|intercluster lifs on two ports or one ifgrp
playbooks.cause: {node} has one intercluster LIF; best practice is two per node.
playbooks.impact: If that LIF or its port fails, replication from the node stops.
steps: 1. Check: network interface show -service-policy default-intercluster -fields address,home-node,home-port

2. Add a second LIF on a different port of {node}: network interface create -vserver {cluster} -lif {node}_ic2 -service-policy default-intercluster -home-node {node} -home-port <port> -address <ip> -netmask <mask>
3. Check the peer sees both: cluster peer show -fields peer-addresses ; network ping -lif {node}_ic2 -vserver {cluster} -destination <remote-ic-ip>
options: Option A: Two intercluster LIFs per node on separate ports or an ifgrp (recommended).

playbooks.match: v3-64bit-identifiers|64-bit nfs v3 identifier|bit nfs v3 identifier for hosting flexgroup
playbooks.cause: SVMs that host FlexGroups ({svms}) use 32-bit NFSv3 file IDs.
playbooks.impact: A FlexGroup with 32-bit identifiers is limited to about 2 billion files.
steps: 1. Plan a window: changing it makes every NFSv3 client see new file IDs, so all clients must unmount and remount to avoid stale file handles.
2. Check (some releases need advanced privilege first: set -privilege advanced): vserver nfs show -vserver {svm1} -fields v3-64bit-identifiers
3. Change: vserver nfs modify -vserver {svm1} -v3-64bit-identifiers enabled
4. Remount on every client, then check access. Repeat for each SVM listed. Return to admin: set -privilege admin
options: Option A: Enable in a planned window with all clients remounted (recommended).
Option B: Leave it if no FlexGroup will approach 2 billion files.

playbooks.match: cluster switch monitoring is not enabled due to switch ip address not reachable
playbooks.cause: ONTAP cannot reach the management address of a cluster switch it should monitor.
playbooks.impact: Switch health is not monitored, so a failing switch port or fan raises no alert.
steps: 1. See what ONTAP has: system switch ethernet show -fields address,is-monitoring-enabled-operational,reason
2. Check the switch management address is reachable from {cluster}'s node management network and that SNMP or the monitoring user is configured on the switch.
3. Correct the address if it changed: system switch ethernet modify -device <switch> -address <ip>
4. Check: system switch ethernet show -fields is-monitoring-enabled-operational ; system health alert show
options: Option A: Fix the address and credentials (recommended).

playbooks.match: do not leave the bootarg\.login\.allowdiag flag set
playbooks.cause: The diagnostic login boot argument is set on {node}.
playbooks.impact: It allows diagnostic-level login with a weaker check, which should only be on while Support is working on the system.
steps: 1. Do one node at a time, with its partner serving data. Check the pair: storage failover show -fields possible,state-description
2. Take the node over: storage failover takeover -ofnode {node}
3. At its LOADER prompt: printenv bootarg.login.allowdiag ; unsetenv bootarg.login.allowdiag ; saveenv ; boot_ontap
4. When the node is waiting for giveback: storage failover giveback -ofnode {node}
5. Repeat for the partner, then check: storage failover show ; system node show -fields health
options: Option A: Clear it in a maintenance window, one node at a time (recommended).

playbooks.match: snapshots are not enabled on all data volumes
playbooks.cause: Some data volumes have no snapshot policy.
playbooks.impact: Without snapshots there is nothing quick to restore from after ransomware or deletion.
steps: 1. List the volumes: volume show -vserver {svm} -fields snapshot-policy,type ; volume show -snapshot-policy none -type RW -fields vserver,volume
2. Use a policy with enough copies (hourly, daily, weekly): volume snapshot policy show -fields schedule1,count1,schedule2,count2
3. Apply it: volume modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -snapshot-policy default  (or your own policy)
4. Reserve space only if needed: volume modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -percent-snapshot-space 5
options: Option A: A policy on every data volume (recommended).
Option B: Replicate to a vault (SnapMirror) for volumes where local snapshots are not wanted.

playbooks.match: volume is hitting the default (?:near )?full threshold|flexgroup volume constituent is over
playbooks.cause: A volume is close to full.
playbooks.impact: At 100% the volume stops accepting writes; clients see "no space" errors.
steps: 1. See the volume: volume show -vserver {svm} -fields size,used,percent-used,autosize-mode,snapshot-reserve-available
2. Let it grow by itself: volume autosize -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -mode grow -maximum-size <size> -grow-threshold-percent 85
3. Or grow it now: volume modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -size +<amount>  (check the aggregate has room: storage aggregate show -fields availsize)

4. Free space: snapshots first, volume snapshot show -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -fields size ; volume snapshot delete ... (only if retention allows), and set volume snapshot autodelete modify -vserver {svm} -volume <volume> -enabled true -trigger volume
5. For a FlexGroup, a constituent filling means imbalance: volume show -vserver {svm} -is-constituent true -fields used ; consider volume rebalance (9.12.1 and later) before growing.
options: Option A: Autosize with a maximum, plus an alert at 85% (recommended).
Option B: Move the volume to an aggregate with more room: volume move start.

playbooks.match: disk firmware is not on the latest revision
playbooks.cause: Some drives run older firmware than NetApp currently ships.
playbooks.impact: Older firmware can carry known drive faults fixed in later revisions.
steps: 1. See what is behind: storage disk show -fields model,firmware-revision -container-type spare,aggregate ; storage disk option show -fields bkg-firmware-update
2. Download the current disk firmware package from the NetApp Support Site (Downloads > Firmware > Disk Drive Firmware) and put it on a web server.
3. Load it on every node: storage firmware download -node * -package-url http://<web-server>/<disk-firmware>.zip
4. The drives update in the background when bkg-firmware-update is true. Watch: storage disk show -fields firmware-revision ; event log show -message-name disk.fw*
options: Option A: Update during low load (background update, non-disruptive).

playbooks.match: sp\/bmc is not running the latest firmware
playbooks.cause: The service processor (SP/BMC) of {node} is not on the latest firmware.
playbooks.impact: Out-of-band management and hardware monitoring run with older, possibly vulnerable code.
steps: 1. See it: system service-processor show -node {node} -fields firmware-version,status ; system service-processor image show -node {node}
2. Let ONTAP update it automatically on the next software install: system service-processor image modify -node * -autoupdate true

3. Or update now: system service-processor image update -node {node} -baseline true  (installs the SP/BMC firmware bundled with the ONTAP release the node runs), or -package <version> for a package you downloaded from the NetApp Support Site (the two cannot be combined). Follow it with: system service-processor image update-progress show
4. Check: system service-processor show -node {node} -fields firmware-version ; system service-processor image show
options: Option A: Turn on auto-update (recommended).

playbooks.match: shelf modules with out-of-date firmware
playbooks.cause: Shelf module firmware is behind the current package.
playbooks.impact: Known shelf module faults fixed in later firmware stay open.
steps: 1. See what the I/O modules run: storage shelf show -module

2. Download the shelf firmware package from the NetApp Support Site (Downloads > Firmware > Disk Shelf Firmware) to a web server and load it on every node: storage firmware download -node * -package-url http://<web-server>/<shelf-firmware>.zip
3. Update (advanced privilege): set -privilege advanced ; storage shelf firmware update -shelf <shelf>  (or -module-type <type> for all shelves with that module). Return with: set -privilege admin
4. Check: storage shelf show -module
options: Option A: Update in a quiet period, one shelf at a time (recommended).

playbooks.match: cve-\d{4}-\d+|vulnerabilit|advisory id: ntap|ntap-\d{8}-\d{4}|susceptible to bug|\bCONTAP-\d+|passed the end of engineering
compact: 1. Upgrade {cluster} to {target|the release that contains the fix}{sameLineNote}: cluster image validate -version {target|<target>} ; cluster image update -version {target|<target>}. One upgrade fixes every finding in the group "ONTAP upgrade to {target|the fixed release}"; the full procedure is in the Implementation Plans.
playbooks.cause: {what} affects the ONTAP release installed on {cluster} ({version|release not reported}); the fix is in a newer release.
playbooks.impact: {recommendation|See the advisory for the impact.}
steps: 1. Read the fix details: {ref|the advisory linked below}. Note the affected and fixed releases and any mitigation NetApp lists for {what}.

2. {?target}Target release: {target}{target2Note}. {cluster} runs {version|an unknown release}.{lineNote}{:}Target release: the first release that fixes {what}; the advisory or bug page below lists it. Prefer a patch on the release line {cluster} runs ({version|unknown}).{/?}
3. Plan it in Active IQ Digital Advisor: Upgrade Advisor creates the plan and lists what to resolve for {cluster} ({node} and its partner).

4. Check health first: cluster show ; storage failover show ; system health status show ; network interface show -is-home false ; snapmirror show -status Transferring ; volume move show ; system node image show
5. Load the image on {cluster}: cluster image package get -url http://<web-server>/<ontap-image>.tgz ; cluster image package show-repository
6. Validate and estimate: cluster image validate -version {target|<target>} ; cluster image update -version {target|<target>} -estimate-only true ; resolve every error it reports.

7. {?metrocluster}This is a MetroCluster: follow NetApp's MetroCluster upgrade procedure (check with metrocluster check run and metrocluster check show before and after; do not start while a switchover is in effect).{:}Update (rolling, one HA partner at a time, no outage for HA pairs): cluster image update -version {target|<target>}{/?}
8. Watch it: cluster image show-update-progress ; cluster image show-update-log
9. Confirm: cluster image show (every node on {target|the target}) ; storage failover show ; network interface revert -vserver * -lif * ; system health status show ; event log show -severity error
options: Option A: Upgrade to {target|the fixed release} in a planned window (recommended).
Option B: If an upgrade cannot happen soon, apply the mitigation in the advisory (restrict access to the affected service on the management network) and record a time-limited exception.
playbooks.thirdParty: Check the NetApp Interoperability Matrix for host, backup and hypervisor integrations on the target release before the window.

ticket.window: Planned maintenance window; rolling upgrade, no outage for HA pairs
ticket.rollback: Going back to the previous release is possible only in the cases NetApp documents (system node revert-to, with Support) and is not offered for every pair of releases; so validate and estimate first, keep the previous image on the nodes (system node image show), and do not use features of the new release until the cluster is confirmed healthy.

playbooks.match: remote login is enabled
playbooks.cause: SSH/Telnet remote login to the controllers of {model} is enabled.
playbooks.impact: Remote login is meant for NetApp Support at their request. Left on, it gives anyone who can reach the controller management network a shell prompt to attack.
steps: 1. Confirm with the storage team that NetApp Support is not working on the array now: remote login is meant for technical support only.

2. In SANtricity System Manager select Hardware, then Controllers and components. Click the controller (the graphic changes to show controllers), then Configure remote login (SSH) in its menu (named Change remote login in SANtricity 11.73 and earlier).
3. Clear the Enable remote login check box and save. Disabling it ends any current SSH sessions and rejects new logins.
4. On a duplex array, if remote login is also enabled on the second controller, a confirmation dialog opens and lets you disable it there too; otherwise repeat for the second controller.

5. If NetApp Support needs it later, turn it on for the session only. On SANtricity 11.74 and later you can require an SSH key, or an SSH key and a password, for remote login (the Authorized public keys list applies to both controllers).
options: Option A: Disable on both controllers (recommended).
Option B: Keep it on only while a support case needs it, and record who turned it off again.

ticket.window: Any; open shell sessions to the controller end
ticket.rollback: Tick Enable remote login again in Configure remote login (SSH) on each controller.

playbooks.match: santricity os \(controller firmware\) has been determined to have a version or configuration exposed
compact: 1. Upgrade {node} to SANtricity OS {target} in System Manager (Support > Upgrade center > Begin SANtricity OS software upgrade). One upgrade fixes every finding in the group "SANtricity upgrade to {target}"; the full procedure is in the Implementation Plans.
playbooks.cause: The SANtricity OS (controller software) on {node} is {version}; NetApp's advisory for {finding} is fixed in a later release.
playbooks.impact: Until the controller software is upgraded the advisories listed for this array stay open.
steps: 1. Read the advisory ({ref}) for the fixed release and any mitigation. The release asked for is SANtricity OS {target}; the array runs {version}.
2. Check the path: systems must be running SANtricity OS 11.70.5 to upgrade to 11.80.x or later, so an older array needs an intermediate upgrade first.

3. Make sure the array is healthy. In System Manager open Home, click the Bell icon, then the Recover from n problems link: the Recovery Guru should list nothing. A hot spare in use, an incomplete volume group, a controller that is not Optimal and similar conditions stop an upgrade.

4. Download the files to your management client: on the NetApp Support site choose Downloads, then Downloads, then E-Series SANtricity OS Controller Software. Digitally signed firmware is required from 8.42, and an unsigned file is rejected. Download the Controller NVSRAM file as well (its name looks like N2800-830000-000.dlp).
5. If the array has one controller, or no multipath driver is installed on the hosts, stop I/O first. A two-controller array with a multipath driver needs no stop.

6. In System Manager select Support > Upgrade center. Under SANtricity OS software upgrade click Begin SANtricity OS software upgrade, Browse to the OS file and to the NVSRAM file. To move the load off peak, tick Transfer files now, but do not start the upgrade (activate later) and activate later.

7. Click Start and confirm. The pre-upgrade health check can be cancelled; transfer and activation cannot. Do not change the array and keep power on while it runs. The controllers fail over during activation, so performance is lower until it finishes.
8. Click Save log for the record (drive_upgrade_log-timestamp.txt).

9. Check: all components show on the Hardware page, and Support > Upgrade center > software and firmware inventory shows the new versions. Custom NVSRAM settings are lost at activation: apply them again.
options: Option A: Upgrade the OS and NVSRAM together in a planned window (recommended).
Option B: Transfer now and activate in the off-peak window.
Option C: Until the upgrade, restrict access to the array's management interfaces to the management network and record a time-limited exception.
playbooks.thirdParty: Check host compatibility in the NetApp Interoperability Matrix Tool before the upgrade. If this array is the storage controller of a StorageGRID appliance (SG5700, SG6000), upgrade SANtricity OS from the Grid Manager instead: Maintenance > System > Software update > SANtricity OS update, after applying the latest StorageGRID hotfix; the NVSRAM is upgraded with it (see the appliance page in the sources).

ticket.window: Planned window; controllers fail over during activation
ticket.rollback: Do not downgrade SANtricity OS on your own: a downgrade is only done as technical support instructs. Validate the files first, keep the pre-upgrade configuration saved, and transfer now/activate later to test on one array first.

playbooks.match: media scan frequency is high
playbooks.cause: Background media scans on {node} are set to run over {days} days.
playbooks.impact: A high media scan frequency may wear certain drive models out sooner than their expected life.
steps: 1. In System Manager select Storage > Volumes, click the ellipsis icon, then Change volume media scan settings. The Change Drive Media Scan Settings window lists every volume.

2. Keep the Media scan check box ticked (clearing it suspends all media scans) and set the number of days over which the scan runs. The default period is 120 days; a longer period lowers the scan rate. Currently {days} days.
3. Keep the Media Scan check box ticked for the volumes that should be scanned. Redundancy Check is enabled with it; untick it only for a volume where a redundancy check is not wanted.
4. Click Save. Media scans run continuously at a constant rate, based on the capacity scanned and the days chosen.
5. Why the scan matters: it finds and repairs media errors on blocks that applications rarely read, using redundancy data, so a later drive failure does not hit unreadable blocks.
options: Option A: Set the period to the default 120 days (recommended) unless a drive model's guidance asks otherwise.
Option B: Keep the shorter period for volumes with data that must be verified more often, and accept the drive wear.

playbooks.match: disk firmware is not on the latest revision|downrev drives|exposed to bug cfdisk|drives rapid media error|new eseries drive firmware risk
playbooks.cause: Drives in {node} run firmware older than the release NetApp lists for them. The finding says: {detail}
playbooks.impact: Older drive firmware can carry known faults (media errors, failures, emissions limits) that a later firmware fixes; some are listed by NetApp as a risk of data loss or an outage.
steps: 1. Note the drive models the finding names. Read the advisory or bug page the finding links for the firmware version that fixes them.

2. Before starting: back up the data (disk-to-disk backup, volume copy to a volume group not affected, or a remote mirror); the array and all drives must be Optimal; no configuration change may be running. If a drive can only be upgraded offline, stop I/O to the volumes that use it.
3. Download the new drive firmware files from the NetApp Support site and unzip them. Files are named like D_HUC101212CSS600_30602291_MS01_2800_0002 with the extension .dlp.

4. In System Manager select Support > Upgrade center, and under Drive firmware upgrade click Begin drive firmware upgrade. Click Browse and choose the files (up to four, one at a time; two files for the same drive model is a conflict, so keep one). Click Next.

5. Choose the type: Upgrade all drives online (drives are upgraded one at a time while the array processes I/O) or Upgrade all drives offline (parallel) (faster, but all I/O to the volumes that use the drives must be stopped). Drives with no redundancy must go offline: that covers SSD cache, RAID 0 volume groups, and any degraded pool or volume group.

6. Select the drives in the first column, click Start and confirm. Do not click Stop unless you must: downloads in progress finish, the rest are cancelled, and stopping can cause data loss or unavailable drives.

7. Click Save log (drive_upgrade_log-timestamp.txt). If an error stops the upgrade (a hot spare in use, an incomplete volume group, a controller not Optimal), open the Recovery Guru (Home > Bell icon > Recover from n problems) and correct it; log, configuration database and MEL errors are for technical support.
options: Option A: Online upgrade for drives that support it, in a quiet period (recommended).
Option B: Offline (parallel) upgrade in a maintenance window for drives that need it.
playbooks.thirdParty: On a StorageGRID appliance (SG5700, SG6000, SG6100) follow the appliance's own drive firmware procedure (see the sources): the appliance may need to be in maintenance mode, and SSDs use the offline method.

ticket.window: Quiet period (online) or maintenance window (offline)
ticket.rollback: A drive firmware upgrade is not reversed from System Manager; check the bulletin for the firmware the finding names, upgrade one array first and watch the Recovery Guru before the next.

playbooks.match: hot spare coverage check
playbooks.cause: No hot spare drive is assigned on {node}, although it has volume groups.
playbooks.impact: If a drive in a RAID 1, 5 or 6 volume group fails there is nothing to rebuild onto automatically, so the group runs without redundancy until a drive is replaced by hand.
steps: 1. Check which drives are assigned: Hardware page; hot spares show as pink drive bays.

2. Choose unassigned drives in Optimal state with the same media type (for example SSD) and interface (for example SAS) as the drives to protect, and a capacity equal to or larger than the used capacity of those drives. Do not assign a drive smaller than the largest drive in the array unless its capacity covers the used capacity.

3. Select Hardware > Drives, click an unassigned (gray) drive, then Assign hot spare. If the drive is secure-enabled, System Manager asks for a Secure Erase first: that deletes everything on it, so check it is the right drive.
4. Confirm the dialog. The drive turns pink. NetApp's recommended coverage is two hot spares per drive set; the finding's own guide is about 2% of the drive count.
5. Pools do not use hot spares: they reserve preservation capacity inside the pool (Storage > Pools and volume groups > ellipsis > Edit Settings), so a pool-only array does not need this.
options: Option A: Assign two hot spares per drive set (recommended).
Option B: Move the data to pools, which reserve preservation capacity instead.

ticket.window: Any; no outage
ticket.rollback: Hot spares are un-assigned from the Hardware page (select the pink drive and remove the hot spare assignment) if the drive is needed elsewhere.

playbooks.match: drawer loss protection is not enabled
playbooks.cause: Volume groups on {node} ({groups}) are not protected against the loss of a drawer.
playbooks.impact: If communication with one drawer of a drive shelf is lost, volumes in these groups can lose access to their data, and cache data can be lost.
steps: 1. See where the drives are: Hardware page, shelf and drawer of each drive of the listed groups.

2. Understand the rule: drawer loss protection is decided by where a group's drives sit. For a volume group it needs drives in at least three shelves or drawers (RAID 1: two); with RAID 5 each drive must be in a separate drawer, and with RAID 6 no more than two in one drawer; RAID 0 cannot have it. For a pool it needs the drives in at least five drawers with an equal number of drives from each. Protection is not guaranteed once a drive in the group has failed.

3. The System Manager pages describe choosing it when a group is created: in Storage > Pools and volume groups, create the group and pick the candidate whose Drawer Loss Protection field shows it is available. NetApp's pages do not describe changing the drive placement of an existing group, so plan a new group of the right shape and a move of the data to it with the application owner.
4. When a drive fails, replace it promptly: a hot spare can take a position that loses the protection, and the copyback after the replacement restores it.
5. When you replace a drive logically (Hardware > Drives > Logically replace), pick a replacement that keeps shelf and drawer loss protection.
options: Option A: Build new volume groups or pools with drawer loss protection and move the data to them (recommended).
Option B: Accept the risk for non-critical data and record an exception.

playbooks.match: recovery guru entries? available
playbooks.cause: {node} reports a condition in its Recovery Guru. The finding says: {detail}
playbooks.impact: The array is not operating optimally; a Needs Attention condition left open can hide the next fault.
steps: 1. In System Manager select Home, click the Bell icon, then the link Recover from n problems at the top centre. The Recovery Guru opens.

2. Select the first problem in the summary list and follow its recovery procedure. Use the replacement instructions where a part has failed. Correct the problems in the order listed, because related problems affect each other. Several failures of a power supply or a fan canister are listed as one problem.
3. Click Recheck to confirm the fix. For an asynchronous mirror group problem click Clear first, then Recheck.
4. The array icon moves from Needs Attention to Optimal when all are corrected; a Fixing icon shows while an operation such as reconstruction runs.
5. Click the Save icon to keep the Recovery Guru details (recoveryGuru-...html) in the change record.
options: Option A: Work through the list now (recommended).

playbooks.match: hdd\(s\) at or over six years of operating life|hdd at or over six years
playbooks.cause: {node} has hard drives that are six years or more old.
playbooks.impact: The expected reliable life of an enterprise hard drive is five years; the likelihood of failure rises the longer it is in service, and a rebuild after one failure stresses the others.
steps: 1. List the old drives and the volume groups or pools they belong to (Hardware page, drive details), and order replacements of the same media type, interface and at least the same capacity.
2. Keep the array healthy meanwhile: hot spares or preservation capacity in place, and the Recovery Guru empty (Home > Bell icon > Recover from n problems).

3. Replace them one at a time with an unassigned drive in Optimal state that has the same attributes: Hardware > Drives, click the old drive, Logically replace, choose the replacement (pick one that keeps shelf and drawer loss protection), and click Replace. The data is copied to the new drive; the old drive goes to Unassigned, or Failed if you ticked Fail drive after it is replaced.
4. Wait for each copy to finish before starting the next.
5. If the whole shelf is old, plan its replacement as a project (migrate the volumes to a new array or shelf) instead of drive by drive.
options: Option A: Replace drives in a planned sequence (recommended).
Option B: Refresh the array or shelf and migrate the data.

playbooks.match: storagegrid webscale has been determined to have a version or configuration exposed|storagegrid.* has been determined to have a version
playbooks.groupKey: StorageGRID upgrade to {target|the recommended release} (fixes security advisories)
compact: 1. Upgrade the grid to {target|the StorageGRID release Active IQ recommends} in Grid Manager (Maintenance > System > Software update > StorageGRID upgrade). One upgrade fixes every finding in the group "StorageGRID upgrade"; the full procedure is in the Implementation Plans.
playbooks.cause: StorageGRID {version} is affected by NetApp's advisory {finding}; the fix is in a later release ({target|the release Active IQ recommends}).
playbooks.impact: Until the grid is upgraded the advisories listed for it stay open.
steps: 1. Read the advisory ({ref}) for the fixed release. Target release: {target|the release Active IQ recommends for this grid (the Upgrade page in Grid Manager shows it)}; the grid runs {version}.

2. Check the installed version: sign in to the Grid Manager and select Help > About. NetApp recommends the latest hotfix for each release before going on to the next, and an upgrade needs the previous major version installed: if the grid is several releases behind, install each upgrade file and its latest hotfix in order. In some cases a hotfix must be applied to avoid a risk of data loss; read the release notes of each.
3. Download the upgrade file (.upgrade) and the hotfix from NetApp Downloads: StorageGRID. If nodes run on Linux hosts, install the RPM or DEB package on every host first.
4. Do not start if the grid is almost full and capacity is urgently needed; finish the upgrade in good time.

5. Select Maintenance > System > Software update, and from the StorageGRID upgrade tile select Upgrade. The Upgrade page shows the recommended path: install the versions and hotfixes in the order shown.
6. Select files: Browse to the upgrade file (and a hotfix file, applied with it); wait for the green check after the code signature check; Continue.

7. Run prechecks: enter the provisioning passphrase, Download recovery package, check you can open it (including Passwords.txt) and copy the .zip to two safe, separate places (it holds keys and passwords). Select Run prechecks and resolve every error; warnings may stay. If custom firewall ports are open, contact technical support before going on.
8. Select Start upgrade. The primary Admin Node is upgraded first (up to 30 minutes) and the Grid Manager is not usable meanwhile (another Admin Node, if online, can show progress).

9. Upgrade the other nodes: download a new recovery package when asked, then Approve nodes. Services on a node stop and the node reboots, so approve only nodes that are ready; approved nodes of one type go one at a time; upgrade a whole site before the next. New features are usable only when all nodes are done.
10. After the last node: the Final upgrade steps finish by themselves (new features within about an hour). Check that services are normal, no unexpected alerts are open, and client connections work.
options: Option A: Upgrade to the recommended release with its latest hotfix in a planned window (recommended).
Option B: Apply the latest hotfix of the current release first when the advisory is fixed there.
playbooks.thirdParty: Check S3/Swift client and load-balancer compatibility with the target release in the NetApp Interoperability Matrix Tool. For appliance nodes the StorageGRID Appliance Installer is updated automatically during the upgrade.

ticket.window: Planned window; each node's services stop and it reboots during its turn
ticket.rollback: A StorageGRID software upgrade is not rolled back by the customer: keep the recovery package, upgrade a site at a time, and contact technical support if a node fails.

playbooks.match: external server ntp redundancy check|less than the recommended .* external ntp servers
playbooks.cause: The grid has fewer than the recommended four external NTP servers.
playbooks.impact: This can result in connectivity issues and services that do not start; if only one node at a site can reach the time sources, timing breaks when it goes down.
steps: 1. Know the design: at each site at least two nodes take the primary NTP role and synchronise to a suggested minimum of four (maximum six) external sources and to each other; every other node is an NTP client of those.

2. Gather the IPv4 addresses of at least four NTP servers that speak NTP, are Stratum 3 or better, and can be reached from at least two nodes at each site. On production, do not use the Windows Time (W32Time) service on a Windows version earlier than Windows Server 2016.
3. Select Maintenance > Network > NTP servers. In the Servers section add, update or remove entries (four to six).
4. Enter the provisioning passphrase and select Save. The page is disabled until the update finishes.
5. If every NTP server fails the connection test after saving, stop and contact technical support.
options: Option A: Four to six servers, reachable from two nodes per site (recommended).

ticket.window: Any; no outage
ticket.rollback: Maintenance > Network > NTP servers: restore the previous list and save with the provisioning passphrase.

playbooks.match: enable compression to conserve space
playbooks.cause: Stored object compression is off on the grid ({node} reports it).
playbooks.impact: Compressible objects use more physical storage than they need.
steps: 1. Check first that it suits the data: do not enable it unless the stored data is compressible. Objects a client already compressed do not shrink further. Do not enable it if NetApp FabricPool uses this grid.

2. Check the clients: with compression on, S3 clients should avoid GetObject calls for a byte range, because StorageGRID has to decompress the object to serve them; such reads can time out, so raise the client read timeout if range reads are unavoidable.
3. Select Configuration > System > Storage settings > Object compression, tick Compress stored objects and select Save. The setting applies in about a minute.
4. Compare storage use before and after on new objects; it does not recompress objects already stored.
options: Option A: Enable for grids storing compressible data and not used by FabricPool (recommended where it applies).
Option B: Leave it off and record why.

playbooks.match: versioning enabled but without .*object lock
playbooks.cause: S3 buckets on the grid have versioning on but no S3 Object Lock.
playbooks.impact: Object versions in these buckets can still be deleted or changed by a user with the permission, which can conflict with retention or compliance rules.
steps: 1. Decide with the data owner which buckets need retention (regulatory, ransomware protection). Object Lock is for those; it is not for every versioned bucket.

2. Grid administrator, once for the grid: enable the global setting (Configuration > System > S3 Object Lock, Enable S3 Object Lock, Apply). It cannot be disabled afterwards, and the default rule of the active ILM policy must be compliant or the change fails.
3. Grid administrator, optional: allow S3 Object Lock for existing buckets, allow Compliance mode for the tenant (otherwise only Governance mode), and set a maximum retention period.

4. Tenant: create new buckets with S3 Object Lock enabled (Tenant Manager, Tenant Management API or S3 API); or, where the grid administrator allowed it, enable it on an existing bucket. Versioning is enabled automatically and cannot be suspended on a locked bucket.
5. Set a default retention mode and period on the bucket if every object should be retained (they apply to new objects only), and set per-object retention from the S3 client where needed.

6. Remember what each mode does: in Compliance mode an object cannot be deleted until its retain-until-date and that date can only be extended; in Governance mode users with the special permission can bypass it.
options: Option A: Enable Object Lock on the buckets that hold retained data (recommended).
Option B: Keep versioning only, and rely on access policy, for data with no retention requirement.

playbooks.match: site .* capacity above|capacity above \d+%
playbooks.cause: A site of the grid is filling up. The finding says: {detail}
playbooks.impact: As Storage Nodes fill, new writes go to the nodes with free space, and ILM placement can no longer be met at the full site.
steps: 1. Look at your ILM rules first: where and when to add capacity depends on how replicated and erasure-coded objects are placed.

2. Choose how to add: more storage volumes to existing Storage Nodes (a software-based node supports up to 48; an SG6060 takes one or two expansion shelves of 16 volumes each, an SG6160 one or two of 60; other appliances cannot add volumes; an existing volume cannot be resized), or more Storage Nodes at the site (no more than 10 in one expansion).
3. Check before you start: no recovery, upgrade or other expansion is running at the site, and all data-repair operations from earlier recoveries are complete.
4. Add enough nodes to keep write performance: writes go in proportion to free space, so a few new nodes next to nearly full ones will carry most of the new writes.
5. Metadata lives on volume 0 only: adding volumes does not add metadata capacity, adding Storage Nodes does.
6. Follow the expansion procedure for the type of node you add, from the expansion guide in the sources.
options: Option A: Add Storage Nodes to the site (also grows metadata capacity).
Option B: Add volumes or expansion shelves to existing nodes when the model allows it.
Option C: Review ILM placement so the site is not holding more copies than the rules need.
